Humans and Light

Dylan Houle

I took these photographs over several nights across Georgia Tech’s campus and Midtown Atlanta. I set out to photograph people and light but ended up with less people than expected which changed my view on the project. In a city at night, you rarely see the people themselves but rather the light they leave behind. Once I noticed that, the emptiness of sidewalks and buildings became the subject.

Every light source in the photos exists because someone decided it should. A lamp marks where to walk. A traffic signal tells people when to stop and when to go. A lit office means someone is still working. A spotlight on the Ramblin’ Wreck shows the importance it holds. A storefront light invites you inside. None of these lights are natural, and each one was planned, installed, and consciously put in place, and each one does a specific job for the people around it.

The sequence of photos attempts to move from small to large. It starts with a single lamp over a sidewalk where Lime bikes sit parked. From there it moves through signals, buildings and symbols and then into the city where the light gets louder and faster: crowded streetlights, office towers, and highway traffic turned into streams of headlights. It ends in the strobe lights of a police cruiser, followed by two final images that pull back from that noise, an empty floodlit tennis court and a dark field at the edge of the city. By the end, human light is no longer contained in the lamps or windows but shown in the colors of the sky, where the clouds glow from the city below.

I want the viewers to notice how much of the night has been built by humans and to see the light as evidence that someone has been there.

Humans and Light. Dylan Houle, 2026.
